newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Philippine peso hammered as rate regime relaxed.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso hammered as rate regime relaxed.

text.p: The Philippine peso fell sharply on Friday after the central bank widened the currency's trading band in a move praised by many analysts.
While the timing of the move took the market by surprise, it was seen as inevitable by many.
"I don't think this was a real surprise considering the peso had been in a managed float in the first place," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.

"What has been surprising is how the managed float was controlled, it has been more like a fixed rate up to now. We, and a lot of other people, expected the peso to depreciate by the end of the year."

The Philippine authorities sprung the news as trading got underway on Friday, saying it would allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar and that the move would allow a gradual cut in interest rates.
The central bank has been defending the 26.40 level and it was quoted there before the news broke.
The peso sank more than 11 percent to a low of 29.45 per dollar in immediate reaction to the news before the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) halted peso-dollar trading onshore today.

A brief straw-poll of currency experts pointed to a settling of the peso around 27 per dollar but some were more bearish and said purchasing power parity calculations pointed to a level nearer 32 to the dollar.
Under BAP rules peso trading is halted when the peso moves beyond 1-1/2 percent of a reference rate. The reference rate was 26.40, the same level the central bank had been defending.

"They have done the sensible thing," CIBC's Chiang said. "Instead of keeping interest rates high and causing growth to slow they have at least given the exchange rate more flexibility and that will allow rates to come down."
The peso came under pressure in the wake of the Thai baht crisis and the Philippine central bank has been forced to intervene and push up interest rates to stop it declining.
However, the peso was really never the subject of an aggressive speculative attack because in the absence of a forward market and an illiquid spot market it was a difficult currency to sell short.

Nevertheless, with less than $12 billion in foreign exchange reserves, analysts had been saying for some time that the Philippines was not in as strong position as, say, Malaysia in defending its currency.
Indeed, during the morning the central bank said it estimated that its currency reserves now stood at only around $10 billion.
While it suffered from a knock-on effect from Thailand, the Philippine economy is better based.

"This knock-on effect has hit a more fundamentally sound and stronger economy in the Philippines but not with the financial reserves to ward off speculation for a long period of time," Bill Belchere, head of fixed income and economic research at Merrill Lynch in Singapore, told Reuters Financial Television.

Since the beginning of 1996, the central bank has kept the peso in less than a four centavo range and analysts said this had led to the currency being fundamentally overvalued and it needed to correct. -- Singapore Newsroom +65-870-3091
